Exercise wasn't randomized. Participants chose whether to train.

Past 50, the muscle comes from lifting heavy things often, eating enough protein and sleeping. Get those three sorted first. Then worry about what's in the shaker.

hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text:
Last week I had a night terror, throwing myself off the bed and bloodying up my back, sides and arms.  

I dreamt that I was on a runaway train and jumped off in a panic.  

I had night terrors years ago but they'd stopped. They were a significant problem in my life as I'd frequently seriously injure myself. I ended up in the hospital once from it. 

I did some research and it seems that they coincide with sleep deprivation. Happening 1-3 hours after sleep onset. 

This makes sense why I had one: I spent five days at 7,000 ft while also missing my bedtime for consecutive days for social events. Going from sea level to altitude creates acute sleep disruption. Full acclimation happens over several weeks. 

People mistakenly think that bad dreams happen in REM but during REM your brain chemically paralyzes your muscular system so you can't act out. 

Night terrors happen during deep slow wave sleep (stage n3) when your muscles aren't paralyzed, putting you at risk of doing something dangerous with your body, like I did.
hits.draft_en:
Bryan Johnson threw himself off the bed in a night terror. His own research pointed at sleep deprivation, a few nights of missing bedtime plus altitude.

That's the bit worth knowing. Short sleep doesn't just make you tired on site. It messes with your brain in ways you don't see coming.

Early starts mean early nights. Guard your bedtime like you guard your knees. The work's still there in the morning.
hits.video_tip: 15–20s face-to-cam, low light or ute at dawn; caption “Short sleep does more than make you tired.” then “Early start = early night.”

hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text:
I reviewed Tobi’s biomarker’s from the car race yesterday. His heart rate, respiration, nervous system, focus, brain state, and more.

It’s insane.

I have some observations below. First, you need to get into the right headspace to understand the insanity.

Imagine this…

> you're breathing at an 8 min/mile (5 min/km) pace
> in a 110°F (43°C) heat chamber 
> heart rate of 145 bpm, peaking at 171 bpm
> intermittently body checked 700 lbs (320 kg) of force
> your core body temp near 102°F (39°C), a high fever
> claustrophobically strapped in a six point harness 
> helmeted head weighs 65 lbs (30 kg) under g load
> no evaporative cooling
> you’ve lost 4.6% of your body mass through sweat
> you can’t move
> vision narrowing from thermal strain and dehydration

Now, in these circumstances, your job is to…

> drive a tightrope at 180 mph (290 km/h)
> overtaking/defending against ahead, beside, behind
> staying within millimeters of tolerance 
> lose concentration for a tenth of a sec, in trouble

Do this for 2.5 hours straight.

A few additional things I find interesting from looking at the data:

1. It’s crazy to me his body can be in such a heightened state while completely stationary. Sitting down, he produced a cardiac load equal to high intensity physical exertion.

2. Thirty minutes before the race, Tobi’s body was already racing. His heart rate elevated to 136 bpm, more than 2x his baseline.

3. In qualifying, the higher his heart rate, the faster his lap. Arousal and performance moved in sync, including his personal best lap.

4. He lost 4.6% of his body mass in sweat. This is severe dehydration. At 2% dehydration your reaction time measurably decreases. He surpassed this in the first hour.

5. His nervous system was switched entirely to fight. There was no chill, anywhere.

6. His incredibly high breathing rate was driven by extreme sympathetic stress and rising core temperature, averaging 41 breaths a minute on his flying laps, moving 93 liters of air a minute.

7. His peak respiratory rate was 59. This is an all out sprint!

8. The only life experience I can map onto Tobi’s experience  was doing 27 mg of 5-MeO-DMT, the world’s most powerful psychedelic. It was all consuming, taking me to the cliff of my physical and mental capacity for 45 minutes. Otherwise, it is very hard for me to imagine being able to excel in these extreme conditions for 2.5 hours.
|
I now understand a little more what Tobi was telling me about the flow state he drops into. Under such extreme physiological conditions, the brain ruthlessly narrows focus. His brain downregulates the self-monitoring prefrontal regions (the self narration). The spike in norepinephrine dilates time, creating the perception of time slowing down.

MRIs on professional drivers show they use roughly one brain region for tasks where novices light up fifteen. A novice would be crushed in these circumstances in less than 10 minutes.

I’m impressed. It’s very hard and nearly impossible to actually understand what it’s like to go through something like this. 

Tobi and @dhh (Tobi’s teammate) were both my first customers at Braintree and gave my startup life when it wasn’t clear if we had a future. They generously encouraged other startups in the Ruby on Rails community to use us.  DHH’s co-founder @jasonfried  did as well. They’ve been great friends to me.

As to Tobi’s performance in the race, he did exceptionally well:

> closed within +0.51% of the fastest Bronze driver, putting him neck and neck with the top ranked amateur drivers in North America

> got his fastest lap of the race on Lap 88 (1:15.359), over two hours in and with peak dehydration and thermal strain, showing incredible tenacity

> finished just +2.60% off absolute class best, competing against world class professionals

There were 150 drivers competing in this race. Respect to all of you. I have a whole new appreciation for the sport.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
I want you to eat blueberries, just not with bananas (unless you really want to).

In my new episode, I examine the evidence for blueberries' benefits on blood flow, brain aging, glucose regulation, gut health, inflammation, and exercise recovery.

Blueberries improve the ability of arteries to relax and deliver blood to the brain, heart, and working muscles. They can improve insulin sensitivity and buffer the blood-sugar response to a calorie-rich meal. Human interventions have also demonstrated improved aspects of memory and cognition in older adults, while observational data link regular blueberry intake to slower cognitive decline.

This isn’t simply an antioxidant story. Blueberry polyphenols act like biological signals, influencing nitric oxide, inflammation, gene expression, and possibly neuronal plasticity.

I also revisit the controversial banana-smoothie question, and explain why I take a cautious approach when my goal is maximizing blueberry-polyphenol exposure.

The full episode is out now on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Enjoy!

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
About 1 in 8 children and adolescents were diagnosed with vitamin D deficiency within a year of starting a GLP-1 drug.

Nearly 17% received at least one new diagnosis of a nutritional deficiency or related complication. Vitamin D deficiency alone affected 12.4%. Yet fewer than one in four received nutrition counseling within six months.

This doesn't prove the medications caused the deficiencies (obesity itself increases the risk of low vitamin D). But GLP-1 drugs suppress appetite by design, and when the body is undergoing rapid growth and development, nutritional sufficiency matters enormously.

Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and skeletal development, along with muscle function, immune regulation, and neurodevelopment.

The takeaway here is not that children should avoid GLP-1 drugs when appropriate. It’s that treatment should include nutrition counseling and monitoring of vitamin D and iron status, protein intake, and growth, not just weight loss.

PS: Adults using GLP-1 drugs should pay attention to micronutrient status, too!

I use exogenous ketones. But not everyday.

I use them strategically, especially before situations when stress could interfere with how clearly I think.

Human studies suggest that exogenous ketones such as beta-hydroxybutyrate may have anxiolytic effects and support cognitive function during stress. One proposed reason is that ketones influence inhibitory signaling involving GABA and adenosine, which may help quiet some of the "mental noise" produced by anxiety.

Before a major presentation or podcast, I'll take about 10 mL of a liquid beta-hydroxybutyrate ester (about 3-5 grams of ketones). For me, it helps calm some of that anxiety and improves my focus and attention.

I view exogenous ketones as a situational tool, not a daily supplement, and I've found them extremely helpful when I need to perform under pressure.

hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text:
Am I a madman or messiah? 

I’m not going to feign humility or pretend I’ve stumbled into this. For 30 years I’ve worked to create something of enduring value for the human race.

My primary education has come from reading biographies. You can read a book on World War II and learn how the Germans did this, and the Americans did that. Autobiographies, by contrast, preserve the high resolution nuance that broad histories discard, capturing the raw psychology and lived friction of the era.

Biographies speak to me because they represent the rare artifacts that survived the brutal compression of time. Every generation’s existence is compressed by around 90%. That means, 90% of people and things that seemed immortal during their time are erased from history in a single generation. It’s simply too much information for humans to carry forward. Three generations of compression means that 99.9% of human activity is forgotten, leaving only one in a thousand figures, ideas, or works to cross the threshold into cultural memory.

Humans solve this information overload by encoding entire epochs into a single person, event, work, institution or idea. These distilled archetypes become required information for the species to tell its own story.

Going deep into biographies in my 20s, I could see these patterns: an infinite depth of human experience continuously compressed into durable memetic code.

I felt inspired by this idea and by the people I was learning about. I specifically admired those, who in their time and place, were able to identify the central defining issue of their time. They didn’t do what others were doing. They didn’t by default pursue the status games of their era. They sought out what I call Zeros.  

Schopenhauer drew this distinction: 

> Talent hits a target no one else can hit. (First principle thinking)

> Genius hits a target no one else can see. (Zeroth principle thinking)

I wondered:
> what will be the Zero of my lifetime? 
> what is currently invisible yet will be the only thing history will see? 
> can I find it and build it? 

I’ve been pursuing this goal since I was 21 years old. Without having any real talent, struggling as a student, having a humble upbringing, and no world connections, I set a goal of becoming independently wealthy by age 30. Then, with money, I reasoned, I’d set my focus on becoming a Zero detective and a Zero builder. 

At age 34, I sold Braintree Venmo in 2013 for $800M, making $300M of that. 

It was now time to become a zero detective.

The problem was that I was cooked as a human. The fourteen years of entrepreneurship, young children, existentially wrestling with my spirituality, and a challenging relationship left me chronically depressed, overweight, inflamed, recently divorced, and without meaning. First, I’d have to rebuild myself to stabilize. Health became my stabilization. I didn't know it then, but the thing I did to survive would turn out to be the thing I was looking for.

I obsessively got to work searching for a Zero. I became a voracious reader and thought about it constantly. I hosted a dozen dinners across the U.S., posing the question to attendees, “Imagine we’re in 2050 and life is extraordinary, what did we focus on in 2016 to make that happen?” I’d carefully write down everyone’s ideas and then after the dinner series, I put them down on a piece of paper, drew a box around them, and then told myself I couldn’t do anything inside the box.

Still, I couldn’t see, feel or hear a Zero. 

I then did a thought experiment that did it for me. I imagined being present in the year 2500 and sat there listening to them converse. They were talking about homo sapiens who lived in the early 21st century and they expressed their gratitude saying “We are grateful for homo sapiens of the 21st century who did __________ and __________.”

What do they say? 

What would survive 500 years of compression? 

I thought about this question for years.

Then one day the answer came to me, they say: “We are grateful for homo sapiens of the 21st century who gave birth to superintelligence and figured out they’d no longer die.” 

Our century compressed into two artifacts.

Superintelligence will be built whether or not I’m around. The other artifact was wide open. It would be a turning point in intelligent life. Transitioning from everyone inevitably dies (YOLO) to we are the first generation who won’t die. Changing everything about how we think about life and death, other people, the planet and our precious, fragile existence. 

Don’t Die is the Zero.

A tectonic shift in human values from being willing to kill themselves and others for power, wealth and status, to valuing existence itself above all other rewards. 

Wanting to live is the most ordinary desire a human has, which makes it a strange thing to call invisible. Very few actually want to die, at least today. Yet almost nobody organizes their life around not dying because for all of history it was unachievable. It makes more rational sense to pursue immediate hedonic, status and power objectives and to lean on the elaborate philosophies the species has made to make peace with death.

The era of Don’t Die will commence in 2030. New age reversal therapies will emerge and AI automation will run our lives, removing the biggest blockers of health: discipline and effort. Death acceptance will vanish as fast as body positivity did with GLP-1s.

(The irony here is that if Don’t Die is a Zero, and it comes to pass, then the 90% compression that has been the rule may stop being the rule.)

Kate and I are building for this. 

We do serious experimentation on health. 
We are performance artists.
We are memetic representations.
We are building a philosophy and ideology.
We are building the infrastructure for the species to turn its attention and power to Don’t Die.

If you’ve ever felt inspired, like me, by people of the past, who were willing to be hated, ridiculed, and dismissed in their pursuit of a Zero, the above should give you motivation. You will have to suffer through a prolonged period trying to find and build a Zero but the reward is being of service to the long arc of intelligent existence in this part of the galaxy.

hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
About one cup of whole blueberries per day is the dose that overlaps most consistently with the positive human evidence.

The clearest benefit is vascular. Blueberries improve endothelial function, the ability of arteries to relax and deliver more blood when tissues need it.

Studies also suggest selected memory benefits in older adults with cognitive vulnerability. Improvements in insulin sensitivity or post-meal glucose handling appear more likely when metabolism is already under strain. Findings for gut health and exercise recovery are promising but less consistent.

Randomized trials have not shown that blueberries prevent dementia, diabetes, heart attacks, or strokes. But one cup (roughly 150 to 180 grams) of fresh or frozen blueberries per day is a practical, evidence-based target with benefits extending well beyond a simple “antioxidant” effect.

I cover all of this and more in the latest episode of the podcast!

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Did you know that a fast actually increases your metabolic rate? It's a myth that your metabolism slows the moment you stop eating. Early in a fast, it actually does the opposite. 

As blood glucose tends to drift down when you stop eating, your body releases more norepinephrine (a close cousin of epinephrine/adrenaline), and your resting energy expenditure climbs up. In healthy adults who fasted for 84 hours, resting energy expenditure rose about 14% by day three, while norepinephrine more than doubled. 

Of course, the more adrenaline and its sibling rise, the more they inhibit insulin release. This further amplifies the metabolic rate effect, insofar as insulin slows metabolic rate very well. 

This is clearly not "starvation mode." There is simply a metabolic cost to your body mobilizing fuel and keeping you alive while you take a break from food.

Jack Ma told Elon Musk humans will always be smarter than machines. 

Musk’s reaction says everything.

“Computers may be very clever, but human beings are much smarter. We invented the computer. I've never seen a computer invent a human being.”

Ma's argument was simple. Computers are tools. They calculate faster, remember more, but humans still hold something machines don't: experience, judgment, wisdom.

Musk clearly didn't buy it. “What would be an example of something that humans are better than a computer at?”

Watching this exchange now feels completely different than it did then. AI agents aren't just calculating anymore. They're writing code, analyzing documents, planning tasks, deciding what to do next on their own.

METR found that the length of software tasks frontier agents can complete autonomously has historically doubled roughly every seven months, with signs of even faster progress through parts of 2024.

That's where Ma's argument starts to buckle. For decades, technology automated what humans did. AI is starting to automate what we assumed required a human to think.

And companies were already learning to create enormous value with almost no people before this wave even arrived. Instagram sold for $1 billion with 13 employees. WhatsApp sold for $19 billion with 55.

Now picture what happens when a small team can direct hundreds of machines that never sleep, never take a salary, never need an office.

The question was never just which jobs disappear.

It's what happens to the money once fewer humans are needed to create it in the first place.

That's the question behind 2028: The Economy Without Humans.

outsiders.name: andrew chen
outsiders.text:
DO  AGENTS  HAVE  NETWORK  EFFECTS?

We are seeing a new wave of general purpose consumer-friendly agents, and it’s causing many thousands of AI startups to re-evaluate their place in the market. Will these new horizontal players take over completely? Will it be winner take all? Can products that focus vertical use cases survive? The new wave of products - Muse, Town, Instinct, Grokbot, etc - come from taking the power and magic of Openclaw/Hermes but wrapping it in polished, secure, consumer-friendly experience. This is only the beginning, and soon every major tech company will throw their hat in the ring and thousands of startups that have been working on vertical agents in X (travel, shopping, family, work, SMB, etc etc) have big existential questions to answer.

[Very long post continues — argues agents don't inherently have network effects but can design them via viral artifacts and shared identity/reputation networks; closes:] The much more consequential question is: Where will the network effects live? If they live primarily in open protocols and specialized networks, we may end up with thousands of agents competing on intelligence, personality, UX, specialization, and price, all interoperating with the same underlying ecosystem. Vertical agents can thrive in this world. But if a few horizontal agents successfully accumulate identity, relationships, private context, reputation, latent intent, and distribution - and keep those assets proprietary - then switching agents starts to mean leaving your network behind. Next couple years will be very fun to see how this plays out.

The new wave of products - Muse, Town, Instinct, Grokbot, etc - come from taking the power and magic of Openclaw/Hermes but wrapping it in polished, secure, consumer-friendly experience. This is only the beginning, and soon every major tech company will throw their hat in the ring and thousands of startups that have been working on vertical agents in X (travel, shopping, family, work, SMB, etc etc) have big existential questions to answer.

[Very long post continues — argues agents don't inherently have network effects but can design them via viral artifacts and shared identity/reputation networks; closes:] The much more consequential question is: Where will the network effects live? If they live primarily in open protocols and specialized networks, we may end up with thousands of agents competing on intelligence, personality, UX, specialization, and price, all interoperating with the same underlying ecosystem. Vertical agents can thrive in this world. But if a few horizontal agents successfully accumulate identity, relationships, private context, reputation, latent intent, and distribution - and keep those assets proprietary - then switching agents starts to mean leaving your network behind. Next couple years will be very fun to see how this plays out.

Claude Opus 5.5 basically rebuilt Terraria in 3D.

8 days.
346K lines of C#.
3,369 items.
313 enemies & bosses.
Custom engine. No Unity. No Godot.

And the wildest part?

The creator says they wrote none of the code.

AI game development is getting absurd.

virals.text:
SpaceXAI engineer, Lauren Tan:

"250 applications, two years, zero offers. Then he stopped applying as one engineer and showed up as one engineer running 30 agents. We offered him $850,000.

Right now I'm running 30+ agents in a loop with /pstack. I shipped 1,000 PRs last month - this month I'll 2x that. I woke up today and 20 had already landed. My job now is to build the team, not write the code.

99% of engineers still run a single chat window. That's not a skill gap. That's a stack gap, and it takes one evening to close."

/pstack → Loop → 30+ Agents → Overnight PRs → Autonomous Workflows

In a 1-hour session, a SpaceXAI engineer explains how to build an effective team of AI agents that works 24/7.

Research → Build → Launch → Improve

It's worth more than any $1000 agentic engineering course.

The Every team runs as much work as possible through agents. To help the whole team share skills when a new model comes out, they built a company agent on Claude Managed Agents that everyone uses in Slack.

Once it caught on internally, they released it to their subscribers.

narrative_synthesis: Outside the health lane, AI talk on X was about AI moving into your home and your hands: personal AI computers (Core ~3M, Oki Home ~723K), an assistant that learns by watching you work (~488K), and AI influencer faces (Higgsfield ~3.7M). The human-versus-machine angle stayed big (Jack Ma to Musk ~903K, Pope Leo pushing back on Nvidia's Jensen Huang over guardrails ~493K, LL Cool J on AI bias ~311K), and so did agents replacing whole teams (Meta's Alexandr Wang on agent swarms ~230K, Claude rebuilding Terraria in 3D ~189K, Lauren Tan's 30-agent loop ~167K). For Tama, the "machines won't replace purpose" and "humans invented the computer" angles fit a worker voice; the product launches are meta only.
